options.why_tempting: take sounds like a peek or a clone, so a would still hold its 3. It moves the value out and leaves None behind.
take wants &mut self, and a is declared mut, so the call is fine. Reading a again afterwards is fine too, because take left a valid value there.
replace hands back the old contents. If you read it as returning what you gave it, c comes out Some(7).
This is replace doing half its job: it returns the old value but forgets to store the new one. It stores it, so a ends as Some(7).

hint: Both methods change a. Track what a holds after each call, and which value each call hands back.

explains.what: take moves the value out of the Option and leaves None in its place, so b gets Some(3) and a is now None. replace puts a new value in and returns what was there before. What was there was None, so c is None and a ends up Some(7).
explains.takeaway: Both methods exist so you can move a value out of something you only have a mutable borrow of. std::mem::take and std::mem::replace do the same job for any type, and they are how you get an owned field out of &mut self without cloning.
